name: Product Development

claims.claim_text: A full-service hardware development engagement spans concept definition and requirements, detailed engineering including schematic capture, PCB design and firmware, field trials and late-stage verification and validation, and then EMC testing, safety testing and product approval.
claims.quote_verbatim: We help with the very front-end doing concept-level stuff, you know, like what will the product look like, feel like, requirements, the fun stuff, the detail engineering, the PCB design, schematic capture, firmware development.
claims.episode_title: Design & Manufacturing Consulting with Scott Williams from Xentronics
claims.speaker: Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: Invention-promotion firms that offer to develop and market an inventor's idea have taken years and tens of thousands of dollars without delivering a product; in one case a mains cord with an inline switch took three years to reach market after two such firms produced nothing and one submission failed safety testing.
claims.quote_verbatim: they took his money, they took two years and they produced nothing
claims.episode_title: China, Entrepreneurs and Blue Collar Reality
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Safety approval for a simple mains product can be obtained directly from a local approval authority for on the order of a thousand dollars, far less than the cost of routing the product through an invention-promotion company.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can go to a local approval authority and pay, you know, a thousand dollars or something and get them to approve it
claims.episode_title: China, Entrepreneurs and Blue Collar Reality
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Soliciting design feedback from an undefined general audience yields comment weighted toward superficial, visible attributes rather than the technical decisions that matter, because only a small fraction of respondents are actual users.
claims.quote_verbatim: you might have a hundred people that say it's great, 10 of whom are actually going to use it in the end and 90 of whom say it needs more LEDs
claims.episode_title: Google Glass, Lean Startup and VotC - Initializing Instructed Interviews

claims.claim_text: Where a subsystem falls outside the team's competence, using a vendor's prefabricated solution or a distributor's field applications engineer trades design ownership for schedule, and is preferred when the objective is shipping the product rather than maximising what the designer learns.
claims.quote_verbatim: sometimes that is, you know, working with a vendor to have a prefab solution
claims.episode_title: Arduino, IndiGoGo and Hack-a-Day - Doodad Dealer Dancing

claims.claim_text: Soft tooling costs substantially less than hard tooling and wears out after far fewer parts, but produces units of high enough quality to function as saleable, testable product well before mass-production tooling exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: you pay a lot less money for soft tools that burn out a lot sooner but that nonetheless allow you to produce pretty reasonable quality products
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy
claims.speaker: Eric Ries

claims.claim_text: Regulated products must be built in prototype form well before mass production, because compliance to standards such as ENERGY STAR has to be demonstrated on physical units.
claims.quote_verbatim: in order to prove that you pass the ENERGY STAR standard and various other regulatory requirements, you have to produce a prototype version much earlier in the process than the one you can mass produce
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy
claims.speaker: Eric Ries

claims.claim_text: In the appliance industry new models historically appeared only every five to seven years, a cadence set by the design time and the tooling investment rather than by demand.
claims.quote_verbatim: new appliances, like really new models, tended to come out like every five to seven years because it took a long time to design
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy
claims.speaker: Eric Ries

claims.claim_text: Most technology platforms exist in a high-production-count and a low-production-count form, such as an FPGA versus a mask-programmed device, allowing early volumes to be served by the more expensive per-unit option.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a high production count and a low production count version of the technology
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy
claims.speaker: Eric Ries

claims.claim_text: Applying a fixed corporate development process that mandates hard tooling to a product whose forecast volume is thousands rather than millions commits a year of tooling work that the volume does not justify.
claims.quote_verbatim: their internal company rules required them to build out the hard tools
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy
claims.speaker: Eric Ries

claims.claim_text: The product concept itself can be validated before the product exists, because customers buy against a representation of what the product is supposed to be, and that representation is the cheapest element to iterate.
claims.quote_verbatim: Almost every customer buys a product based on your version of what it's supposed to be, which is the easiest thing to iterate on the world.
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy

claims.claim_text: An experienced designer taking a product from concept through to production has budgeted around a year, or eleven to twelve months, for the whole path.
claims.quote_verbatim: how a product's taken from concept through to ultimate production. And it's going to take her a year
claims.episode_title: Specialized and/or Open Source Test Gear and Dev Boards - Vacation Videography Vorboten

claims.claim_text: Defects that survive into a production run are discovered only once units are in customers' hands, and the cost of replacing them scales directly with how many were shipped before the defect was found.
claims.quote_verbatim: there were all kinds of bugs that I didn't hash out until I sold 100 of them
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scott Driscoll - Impacable Interdisciplinary Inventor
claims.speaker: Scott Driscoll

claims.claim_text: Reselling commodity products is a low-margin business with almost no barrier to entry, so developing proprietary products is the route to margin that is not set by suppliers' prices.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's why I'm so keen about making our own products because you're not beholden to suppliers' prices.
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi

claims.claim_text: Engineering team composition on connected products has shifted away from hardware, with one company moving from a hardware-led team to roughly one hardware engineer, four firmware engineers and five software engineers, because software and firmware can be changed after the product ships.
claims.quote_verbatim: the shift became one hardware engineer, four firmware people, and, you know, five software
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: The Apple Lisa took about five years to develop, from work starting around 1977 to release in January 1983.
claims.quote_verbatim: it took apparently five years to actually develop that machine from when they first started work on it to when they actually released it in, uh, January, 1983
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A product design cycle of under two years, with eighteen months as the commonly cited figure, has long been treated as the benchmark for consumer and instrument products.
claims.quote_verbatim: 18 month kind of, you know, ballpark
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: Using a trade show as a development milestone forces a working prototype to exist by the show date, which historically produced demonstration units held together well short of production quality.
claims.quote_verbatim: it ends up being this big milestone to actually get a working prototype at CES
claims.episode_title: MightyHohm For The Holidays - Kaiser Keyzer's Kits

claims.claim_text: In large corporate research laboratories the dominant pattern was to staff a product programme, run it for about two years and then cancel it, so that very few projects from a laboratory of several hundred engineers became products anyone could buy.
claims.quote_verbatim: start a project, you know, start a product, get people on it, work it for two years, cancel
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout

claims.claim_text: The next-bench method of product definition is to build a tool that solves a real problem for a colleague at the adjacent bench, which supplies a local customer and rapid feedback on whether the work is worth doing.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'd develop a tool that would solve a problem for the guy over on the next bench
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson

claims.claim_text: A single underlying technology programme ran for sixteen years before it was incorporated into a shipping product.
claims.quote_verbatim: we worked on for 16 years before it actually got into a product
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson

claims.claim_text: The value of a product is the idea multiplied by the execution, so a strong idea executed poorly is worth very little and learning to execute is the critical skill.
claims.quote_verbatim: the value of something is really the idea times the execution
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout

claims.claim_text: For products going out to customers, most of the execution effort falls in the final tenth of the project, covering elements such as packaging and customer response, and that is where projects fail.
claims.quote_verbatim: 90% of your execution better be in the last 10% of that project because that's when it fails
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout

claims.claim_text: Consulting revenue can only be scaled by working longer hours or charging more, both of which have limits, which is the structural reason consultancies develop their own products.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only way you can really scale if you're just doing consulting type work is either work longer hours or charge more
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios
claims.speaker: Bob Davidson

claims.claim_text: Most engineering work is development rather than research, consisting of optimisation and part selection rather than novel investigation.
claims.quote_verbatim: development is optimizing. It's finding better parts.
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Products that require a firmware update immediately out of the box do so because firmware was still unfinished when the units were manufactured.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the reasons that you have to often have to update the firmware right out of the box is because the product isn't finished when they manufacture it

claims.claim_text: Building one unit, ten, a hundred and a thousand are materially different problems, and the step most often skipped is selling ten units to establish that anyone will buy the product at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first step is always sell 10 of them

claims.claim_text: A field-emission display programme reached 99 percent pixel yield across the array and still failed as a product, because the human eye detects the remaining 1 percent of dead pixels.
claims.quote_verbatim: we could get like 99% yield on the pixels in the array, but that 1% your eye could pick up
claims.speaker: Jake Baker

claims.claim_text: Assembling a first prototype from off-the-shelf modules and putting it in front of a customer immediately is a deliberate method for testing whether the concept makes sense before committing development time.
claims.quote_verbatim: the most important thing is getting anything in front of the customer right away

claims.claim_text: Developing for months before showing anything to a customer risks completing a product the customer does not want.
claims.quote_verbatim: you shouldn't go develop something for six months

claims.claim_text: Moving from a working idea or prototype into production consumes a large number of engineering hours, and that cost has to be justified against the size of the market for the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: now to get it from this idea and this prototype into production is like actually many, many, many engineering hours

claims.claim_text: Ideas are abundant and cheap; the work of product development lies in selecting the right one, reducing it to practice and carrying it to market.
claims.quote_verbatim: the challenge is picking the right one, reducing the practice, doing it in the right way, and getting it to market
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang

claims.claim_text: The mechanical and finish details of a polished product must be settled before the order is placed, because unlike much of the electronics they cannot be corrected later.
claims.quote_verbatim: it really has to be solidly nailed down from the get go before you push that order button
claims.episode_title: Fake it till you make it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Taking a design into actual production is where the effort concentrates: the last twenty percent of the design work accounts for roughly eighty percent of the total work.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's like the last 20% of the design effort, that's like 80% of the work.
claims.speaker: Jason Cerundolo

claims.claim_text: A low-volume product is not a priority for its contract manufacturer, so build slots take time and component shortages are often communicated only at the last moment.
claims.quote_verbatim: my product's not a priority for them

claims.claim_text: Once the engineering NRE for a product has been spent, the return comes from the ongoing maintenance and reordering phase, which in small operations remains manual spreadsheet work repeated for every build.
claims.quote_verbatim: the maintenance stuff is how you that's how you make your money

claims.claim_text: Semiconductor vendors release large numbers of similar amplifiers and data converters because no single part can optimise every parameter, so each permutation of specifications answers a customer requirement an existing part misses.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't optimize all the parameters. So, if you think of the different permutations, it does end up creating a need for a lot of parts
claims.speaker: Art Kay

claims.claim_text: Product development requires leaving the office to talk not only to customers but to the manufacturers, because physical distance from the production floor removes context and control over what is actually being built.
claims.quote_verbatim: you just got to get out there and not only get out there and talk to your customers, but get out there and talk to your manufacturers

claims.claim_text: Announcing that a product is being discontinued reliably generates a wave of orders, and interest in a niche product can revive without any marketing activity.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's a great way to actually get people to order something, by the way, is to announce obsolescence.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A designer involved across all stages of development makes product decisions that are a function of how the item will be manufactured as well as how it is designed.
claims.quote_verbatim: you get to make these choices about the product that are a function of not just how it's designed, but how it's going to be manufactured
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: A manufacturing plant's established practice resists processes it has not used before, so a designer proposing an unfamiliar approach is routinely told the line has not done it that way in decades.
claims.quote_verbatim: we haven't done it like that in 20 years
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The staged hardware programme runs proof-of-concept prototyping first, then an industrial design and user-interaction track and a separate engineering track, before the two are merged.
claims.quote_verbatim: we call proof of concept prototype development, which most companies have done by the time we've seen them
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: The engineering track of a hardware programme comprises writing specifications, detailed engineering design, component qualification, and physical testing such as drop testing to confirm the product survives handling.
claims.quote_verbatim: writing specs and, um, and, and sort of detailed engineering design, you know, component qualification and, uh, you know, somewhat rigorous testing around making sure the product is going to survive and can be dropped
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: The industrial design track produces a looks-like prototype and the engineering track produces one or more works-like prototypes; fusing them into a single engineering prototype is the hardest and longest part of the programme, taking many months.
claims.quote_verbatim: that is the, by far the hardest part of the process to go from these two sort of idealistic models into one that, that is a functional product
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Development obligations do not end at the point of sale; returns and post-sale support are part of the programme and are commonly forgotten in hardware planning.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're not done when you sell the product
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: Early production is typically run in-house before transferring to a manufacturer, at volumes ranging from five or ten units at a time up to about a hundred units a week shipped to customers.
claims.quote_verbatim: sometimes it's, you know, five and 10 units at a time. And sometimes we have companies that build a hundred units a week
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: A hardware programme requires mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, embedded systems development, industrial design, and manufacturing and test prototype builds as distinct staffed disciplines.
claims.quote_verbatim: covering mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, embedded systems, development, industrial design, uh, manufacturing and test prototype builds
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: A hardware accelerator's structured engagement with a company runs on average about eighteen months.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's about 18 months, maybe a little bit longer, uh, with companies
claims.speaker: Ben Einstein

claims.claim_text: 3D printing has become a standard part of the consumer product development process, used heavily during design even though it is not a mainstream consumer activity.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would challenge you to find a single consumer product that's designed today that doesn't make heavy use of 3D printing in the product development process
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: The digital picture frame was developed in 1999 and brought to market in 2000, debuting at the Photo Marketing Association trade show and reaching retail distribution.
claims.quote_verbatim: So we developed that in 1999.
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: Published specifications change during development, and the final numbers are often only settled at the point the production manual is written, well after prototypes have been circulated against provisional specifications.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's interesting how the specs actually change.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Early prototypes are circulated with unfinished cosmetics, including hand-applied labels over front-panel controls and no final silkscreen, so that form factor can be evaluated before artwork is frozen.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it's like not finished silkscreen or anything yet.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A precision current-measurement instrument developed by a solo consultant took over two years to reach a first product.
claims.quote_verbatim: the initial Julescope took me, what, over two years to develop
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: A consultant developing an in-house product can schedule it as an internal client with carved-out time, accepting that it ranks below paying clients and that the unbilled hours are a direct opportunity cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: I carved out a little bit of time to start working on what will become my product and treated it just like any of my other clients, although it was really the lowest priority client
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: The function of most prototypes is to demonstrate that an idea is unworkable, which is why a prototype precedes committing to full product development.
claims.quote_verbatim: The role of most prototypes is to show that an idea is unworkable because most ideas are, are unworkable.

claims.claim_text: Reaching a working prototype represents only about twenty percent of the total effort of a hardware product development programme.
claims.quote_verbatim: right now we have 20 percent have done on the whole product development process
claims.speaker: Saber Kaygusuz

claims.claim_text: The effort remaining after a prototype exists consists of certification, transferring to production and working with manufacturers, all of which take substantial time.
claims.quote_verbatim: all the another processes like certification going to production talking to manufacturers everything they're taking a lot of time
claims.speaker: Saber Kaygusuz

claims.claim_text: The share of total effort represented by the prototype depends on product complexity, ranging from around fifty percent for a simple product down to a few percent for a complex one.
claims.quote_verbatim: going to 50 percent by prototype or to two percent
claims.speaker: Saber Kaygusuz

claims.claim_text: Build quantities of around five hundred units are needed to reach component and assembly price breaks, which ties up a large amount of cash for a small company.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have to get to 500 to get you know price breaks and all that other stuff as well and it's just like yeah it's a huge cash flow tie-up

claims.claim_text: By the time a design reaches manufacturing it differs from the original development-board prototype in almost every respect, so an Arduino-based demonstrator establishes feasibility but not the manufacturable product.
claims.quote_verbatim: by the time you're in manufacturing, what you build is very different from that original Arduino prototype by almost every measure
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The difficulty in a seemingly simple product lies in the corner cases of deployment: sensor contamination, ingress protection, getting a radio signal out of a metal enclosure, and remote firmware update.
claims.quote_verbatim: What if the ultrasonic sensor gets dirty? What if, what about ingress?
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams
claims.speaker: Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: Customer requirements typically arrive as a one-line product concept, and the engineering content is in the constraints attached to it, such as an aggressive cost target set by a competitor or survival in an extreme environment.
claims.quote_verbatim: it needs to be ultra low cost because we're trying to rate our competitor
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams
claims.speaker: Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: Development work has shifted toward integrating an existing, refined sensor module rather than designing a custom board around the raw sensor, moving the effort into communication, power and application integration.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not that we're going to design a PCB that has a specialized sensor on it
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams
claims.speaker: Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: A turnkey design house takes a customer from concept through to production and even marketing over an engagement of a year or two, in contrast to services-only partners who supply a single discipline such as a firmware team.
claims.quote_verbatim: it means basically you do the whole job from concept through to production and even marketing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Developing an own-brand product generates no revenue until the product is finished and shipping, unlike client work which is billed as it is performed.
claims.quote_verbatim: you don't earn any income until that product's finished and shipping
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Large corporations pipeline product development so that successive releases track the semiconductor process cadence, producing yearly improvements an individual developer cannot match.
claims.quote_verbatim: they pipeline their product development such that they worked with Moore's Law basically to their advantage
claims.episode_title: Moore's Law, GaN and SiC devices - Gallimaufry GaN Gabble

claims.claim_text: In a small catalogue company any engineer can propose a product, the group reviews candidates together, and a product that sells modestly may be retained on judgement rather than a hard financial metric.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're small and agile enough that we'll actually try it and see, see what happens
claims.episode_title: An Interview with the SparkFun Team - Efficacious Engineering Ensemble

claims.claim_text: Products that begin as a tool built for the designer's own use, and are only recognised as products afterwards, are a common and more reliable origin than starting from the intent to create a product.
claims.quote_verbatim: we hacked it together and then realized that it would be very useful
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk

claims.claim_text: One route to a product is to locate an existing similar item and its manufacturer and commission a variant, which is faster than starting from scratch but forgoes the differentiation that an original design provides.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll find something similar and then they'll go find the manufacturer and be like, can you make something similar to, for me?
claims.episode_title: Inspirations and Aspirations - Recanting Rocket Rationale
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Designing around available development boards and existing software libraries is standard practice, with custom engineering reserved for the parts that differentiate the product.
claims.quote_verbatim: We design around development boards
claims.episode_title: Glass and Gongkai GSM - Unzymotic Ursidae Upbuilding
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Offshore production is not a hands-off transfer; skilled engineers on the manufacturing side still have to shepherd the product through production, and that knowledge remains necessary to the developing company.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's skilled engineers over there that are shepherding the product through production

claims.claim_text: Among the hardest skills in product development is knowing the market: what it wants and what it expects in price and features.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the hard skills is knowing what the market is, knowing what the market wants, what the market will expect in terms of price and features

claims.claim_text: A non-technical customer who inserts themselves into board bring-up, wanting to power up and test the first article personally, disrupts the process and typically forces the engineering team to travel to the customer site.
claims.quote_verbatim: wants to insert themselves into the product development process

claims.claim_text: Working in an organisation of roughly 150 people rather than a several-thousand-person division required covering every step from conceptualisation through shipping and support, giving exposure to the whole product development process.
claims.quote_verbatim: it had to cover every step of design from conceptualization to shipping and support
claims.episode_title: Lee Felsenstein: The Computer Revolution & Counterculture
claims.speaker: Lee Felsenstein

attribution_notes: ep 14: passage labelled Chris Gammell, but the content is Australian throughout (the EcoSwitch, 'here in Australia', the Australian dollar exchange rate) and is the Australian host's story; content-attributed to Dave Jones.

ep 159: the soft-tooling and appliance-cadence passages are the interview guest's own consulting anecdotes and are attributed to Eric Ries by content despite the unreliable-attribution flag. The follow-on passage about selling a product that does not exist yet is labelled Dave Jones but is the same guest still speaking; the name was dropped.
ep 168: the concept-to-production duration passage refers to a third party's schedule; no speaker name carried through.

ep 229: the Apple Lisa teardown passage is labelled Chris Gammell but the content is the person rendering an EEVblog teardown video; content-attributed to Dave Jones. The CES-milestone passage in the same episode is labelled Chris Gammell but the content is the guest describing his own employer; the name was dropped.

ep 232: Bob Davidson is retained for the HP next-bench and 16-year-technology claims (content is consistent with his HP background) and Dave Vandenbout for the large-lab cancellation and idea-times-execution claims; the 'development is optimizing' passage had a name that could not be confirmed against content and was left unattributed.
ep 293: source speaker label is the placeholder SPEAKER_00; no name recorded.
ep 342: passage labelled Chris Gammell but the microcurrent content belongs to the other host; rather than assert a swap, the name was dropped for both claims from this episode.
ep 527: episode flagged unreliable, but the content identifies the JouleScope developer beyond doubt; Matt Liberty retained.
ep 550: passage labelled Chris Gammell, but the content is the guest's thesis on prototyping in an episode about his prototyping practice; the name was dropped.

ep 608: the twenty-percent figure appears in two passages with different speaker labels; the claim cites the passage where the guest states it about his own products and is attributed to Saber Kaygusuz. The 500-unit price-break claim comes from the host-labelled passage and was left unattributed.
ep 614: passage labelled Dave Jones but the content is the consultant describing his own clients and site visits; the name was dropped.
ep 624 and 645: both flagged unreliable, but the content is the speaker describing his own consultancy and its projects; Scott Williams retained.
ep 682 and 61: host-labelled passages where the two hosts' turns interleave; names dropped as the claims are ordinary facts.
